Alabama Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Alabama house?

Check the statute and talk to a Alabama attorney about your facts.

What does Alabama law say about squatters and adverse possession?

Alabama treats squatting and adverse possession as two separate subjects. Adverse possession is a long-running claim to title, governed by a statute in Title 6 of the Code of Alabama. Squatting, in the 2024 sense, is a fast removal procedure for people who walk into a dwelling with no right to be there, found in Chapter 9B of Title 35.

The two rarely overlap in practice. A person who broke into a vacant house last month has no realistic title claim, but the owner still needs a lawful way to get that person out. A person who has occupied a lot for decades and paid tax on it may have a real claim, and removal paperwork will not make it go away.

If you own an Alabama house and someone else is living in it, the first job is to work out which situation you are in. That answer decides whether you file a sworn affidavit with law enforcement, bring a court action, or talk to a title attorney before you sign a sale contract.

What must a person show to claim Alabama land by adverse possession?

Under Alabama Code section 6-5-200, adverse possession cannot confer or defeat title unless the claimant proves one of three things. Mere occupation is not enough on its own.

  • A deed or other color of title that purports to convey the land was recorded with the county probate judge for 10 years before the lawsuit began.
  • The claimant, and anyone the claimant takes through, listed the land for taxation in the proper county every year for 10 years before the action, if the land is taxable.
  • The claimant received title by descent or devise from a predecessor who was in possession.

Time can be stacked. If the claimant's recorded paper and the recorded paper of those he claims through add up to 10 years, he can rely on it. An honest failure to list the land for tax, a slip in the description on the assessment, or an accidental omission of part of the parcel does not by itself defeat the claim during that period.

The section also carries a savings clause. It does not disturb a title that was already perfect by adverse possession before the Code was adopted, it keeps rights under sections 6-6-286 through 6-6-289, and it does not change how disputes over boundaries between neighbors are handled.

Path to a claimWhat the statute requiresPeriod
Color of titleDeed or other paper recorded with the county probate judge10 years before the action
Tax listingLand listed for taxation each year in the proper county, if taxable10 years before the action
InheritanceTitle by descent or devise from a predecessor who was in possessionNo separate period stated in the section

How does an Alabama owner remove a squatter from a dwelling?

An owner, or the owner's agent, can ask law enforcement in the county where the dwelling sits to remove an unauthorized person by submitting a sworn affidavit under section 35-9B-2. The chapter was added by Act 2024-237 and uses the criminal code's definition of a dwelling.

The affidavit is a statement under penalty of perjury. It has to say several things at once, and each one has to be true for your situation:

  • You are the owner of the dwelling or the owner's agent.
  • Someone entered and remains in the dwelling unlawfully and was never authorized to be there.
  • The person is not a tenant and not a holdover tenant.
  • You asked the person to leave and the person has not.
  • The person is not an immediate family member of the owner.
  • No litigation about the dwelling is pending between you and that person.

The statutory form adds more. It says any lease the person produces is fraudulent, that the person is not on title unless title fraud occurred, that notice was hand delivered or posted on the front door with proof of the date and time attached, and that you attach a copy of your government-issued identification or, if you are an agent, papers showing your authority.

Before you file, you must post or hand deliver a notice at the dwelling telling the person to leave immediately. The notice has to give the street address of the law enforcement agency where the affidavit will be delivered, and a copy goes with the affidavit.

What does law enforcement do after it receives the affidavit?

The agency first checks that you are the record owner or the owner's authorized agent and that you appear entitled to relief. After at least 24 hours from receipt, it serves a notice to vacate immediately. Service can be by hand delivery to anyone occupying the home or by posting on the front door. This comes from section 35-9B-3.

Officers also try to identify everyone in the dwelling and record the names on the return of service. If appropriate, an officer may arrest a person found inside for trespass, burglary, theft, another crime, or an outstanding warrant. The agency may charge no more than $50 to process the affidavit.

StepWho actsSource
Post or hand deliver notice at the dwellingOwner or agent35-9B-2(c)
Submit sworn affidavit with ID and notice proofOwner or agent35-9B-2(a), (b)
Verify record owner, wait at least 24 hours, serve notice to vacateLaw enforcement35-9B-3(a)
Identify occupants, arrest if warrantedLaw enforcement35-9B-3(a)
Processing fee of no more than $50Law enforcement agency35-9B-3(b)

What happens if the affidavit is wrong or the removal is wrongful?

The affiant carries the risk. Under section 35-9B-6, a person who is wrongfully removed can sue the affiant. The remedies include getting possession of the dwelling back, actual costs and damages, punitive damages of triple the fair market rent of the dwelling, court costs and reasonable attorney fees.

The affidavit form itself warns about this. The affiant acknowledges that a removed person may bring an action for false statements or for wrongfully using the procedure, with liability for actual damages, penalties, costs and attorney fees. If you are unsure whether the occupant is a tenant, a guest or a relative, get legal advice before signing.

Chapter 9B also protects utilities that rely on the usual court route. Under section 35-9B-7, a utility may rely on or require a writ of possession from the landlord tenant or ejectment chapters when it discontinues or refuses to discontinue service at a dwelling, and it is not liable if it acts on that writ. Turning off power yourself to push someone out is not a safe shortcut.

When the occupant is a tenant or holdover rather than a squatter

The squatting affidavit is closed to tenants and holdover tenants by its own terms. If the person once had a lease, paid rent, or stayed after a term ended, the owner has to use the landlord tenant process in Chapter 9A and file for possession in court.

Under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a landlord can bring an action for possession against a tenant who stays without consent after the term expires or the lease is terminated. A willful holdover can lead to recovery of up to three months of periodic rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees.

This split matters in a sale. A buyer or lender will want to know whether anyone has a recorded claim, a lease, or a court case pending, because the squatting affidavit is unavailable whenever litigation about the dwelling is already pending between the owner and the occupant.

How do squatters and adverse possession affect selling an Alabama house?

An occupied house can still be sold, but the sale path depends on who is inside. The occupant question affects who can buy and how fast.

Three checks help before you list or take a cash offer:

  • Pull the recorded documents at the county probate office. Adverse possession paths run through recorded deeds and tax listing, so a strange recorded instrument or tax history on your parcel is worth knowing about.
  • Write down how the occupant got in and when. The affidavit and any court filing both depend on a clear timeline.
  • Keep the notice, proof of delivery and any police paperwork in one folder.

If the person living there has no claim, Chapter 9B gives you a path. If the person has a lease, a family tie, or a pending case, the path is court. Either way, you can ask us for a cash offer on the house in its current condition, and we will tell you plainly what an occupant does to timing.

More questions about Alabama Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

Can a squatter take ownership of my Alabama house?

Only by meeting section 6-5-200. A claimant has to show recorded color of title for 10 years, annual tax listing for 10 years, or title by descent or devise from a predecessor in possession. Simply living in a house for a while does not transfer ownership.

Is there a faster way to remove a squatter in Alabama than a full eviction?

Yes, for people who are not tenants. Chapter 9B lets an owner or agent file a sworn affidavit with local law enforcement, which verifies ownership, waits at least 24 hours and then serves a notice to vacate. It does not apply to tenants, holdover tenants or immediate family.

How much can law enforcement charge to process a squatter affidavit?

An agency may charge no more than $50 to process the affidavit under section 35-9B-3(b).

What happens if I file the affidavit against someone who is really a tenant?

You can be sued. A wrongfully removed person may recover possession, actual damages, triple the fair market rent as punitive damages, court costs and attorney fees under section 35-9B-6.

Can I shut off the utilities to make someone leave?

Do not rely on that. Section 35-9B-7 says a utility may rely on or require a writ of possession when deciding whether to cut service at a dwelling, so the court process or the affidavit process is the lawful route.

Can I sell my Alabama house while someone is occupying it without permission?

Ownership is what lets you sell, so if you hold title you can contract to sell, but an unresolved occupant affects terms and timing. Ask an Alabama attorney which removal route fits your facts before you sign a contract.

Alabama Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Landlord must refund the deposit or deliver an itemized list of deductions within 60 days after termination of the tenancy and delivery of possession; the tenant must give a written forwarding address; if the landlord fails to mail a timely refund or accounting, the landlord owes double the original deposit. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-201(b)-(f); source)
  • Landlord entry: at least two days' notice, at reasonable times; posting a note on the primary door is a permitted method of notice; entry without consent allowed in an emergency, by court order, or on reasonable belief of abandonment. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-303(b)-(c); source)

Get My Cash Offer →

Which Alabama law governs residential landlords and tenants?

Residential rentals in Alabama fall under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, found in Title 35, Chapter 9A of the Code of Alabama. The Act was passed as Act 2006-316 and has been amended several times since, with changes recorded in 2009, 2011, 2014 and 2018 on the section that covers unpaid rent.

The chapter is organized into six articles, which is a handy map when you are looking for a rule:

  • Article 1, general provisions and definitions
  • Article 2, landlord obligations
  • Article 3, tenant obligations
  • Article 4, remedies
  • Article 5, retaliatory conduct
  • Article 6, effective date, savings clause and severability

Squatting is handled in a separate chapter, Chapter 9B, which is outside the landlord and tenant act. If someone is living in a property with no lease and no permission, that chapter is the starting point rather than the rental rules.

What must a landlord disclose, and who inherits that duty when the property is sold?

Under section 35-9A-202, a landlord or anyone authorized to sign a lease for the landlord must tell the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, who manages the property and who the owner or the owner's agent is for service of process and notices.

Two details stand out for a seller. First, the information has to be kept current. Second, the section states that it extends to and can be enforced against any successor landlord, owner or manager. In plain terms, a buyer of a rental steps into the disclosure duty, and the seller who is leaving should hand over a clean record of what the tenant was told.

The statute also attaches a penalty to silence. A person who fails to comply becomes an agent of each landlord for receiving notices and demands, and for performing the landlord's obligations under the chapter and the rental agreement. That can pull a former owner or a distant owner into disputes they thought they had left behind.

What repairs does an Alabama landlord have to make?

Section 35-9A-204 sets the landlord's maintenance duties. The landlord must follow building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety, make the repairs needed to keep the unit habitable, and keep common areas clean and safe.

  • Keep electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating and air-conditioning systems, and supplied appliances, in good and safe working order.
  • Provide receptacles for garbage and arrange for its removal.
  • Supply running water, reasonable amounts of hot water and reasonable heat, unless the building is not required to have heat or the tenant controls the system through a direct public utility connection.

If a code duty is greater than any other duty in the list, the code duty controls. A tenant loses these rights when the condition was caused by the willful or negligent act of the tenant, a family member or a guest.

Can a tenant agree to do repairs?

Sometimes. For a single-family home, the landlord and tenant may agree in writing that the tenant takes over the garbage and water duties and specified repairs, maintenance, alterations and remodeling.

For any other kind of dwelling, the rules are stricter. The agreement has to be in a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration. The work cannot be needed to cure a code violation, and it cannot reduce the landlord's duties to other tenants. The landlord also cannot make the side agreement a condition of the rental agreement itself.

This matters when you sell a house you rented to a tenant who handles upkeep. A buyer will want to see that written agreement, since the statute calls for one.

How does an Alabama landlord end a lease for unpaid rent or a lease violation?

Section 35-9A-421 lets a landlord send a written notice to end the lease. The notice must set a termination date not less than seven business days after the tenant receives it, and the tenant has until then to fix the problem.

SituationWhat the statute says
Material noncompliance with the leaseWritten notice that specifies the acts or omissions, ending the lease on a date at least seven business days after receipt, unless the tenant remedies the breach first
Unpaid rentWritten notice that states the rent and any late fees owed, with termination not less than seven business days after receipt if the amount is not paid
Intentional misrepresentation of a material fact in the lease or applicationMay not be remedied or cured
Overlap of the two groundsThe unpaid rent period governs

The landlord may also recover actual damages and reasonable attorney fees, and may seek an injunction, for a tenant's noncompliance.

Which tenant breaches cannot be cured?

The same section limits how often a tenant can cure. A breach of the lease may not be cured by a tenant more than two times in any 12-month period unless the landlord gives written consent.

Certain acts are treated as noncurable defaults, and the landlord may end the lease on a seven-day notice with no right to remedy unless the landlord agrees:

  • Making, growing, importing, moving, possessing, furnishing, giving out or using illegal drugs in the unit or the common areas.
  • Illegal use, manufacture, import, possession, furnishing or discharge of a firearm or ammunition on the property, apart from self-defense and the other cases the statute names.
  • Criminal assault of a tenant or guest on the property, again apart from self-defense and the listed exceptions.
  • A second breach involving substantially the same acts as one already noticed and cured, if it happens within six months of the first.

What does this mean when you want to sell a rental house?

Selling a house with tenants in Alabama takes some paperwork, and the statutes above set the baseline. A buyer's attorney or title company will usually look at the lease, the disclosure information, the repair history and any pending notices before closing.

Before listing or taking an offer, gather these items:

  • The signed lease and any written maintenance agreement for the tenant.
  • The written disclosure of the manager and owner or agent given to the tenant.
  • Copies of any termination notice, including the date the tenant received it, since the seven business day count starts at receipt.
  • A record of repairs made under the landlord's duties and any code notices.

A tenant in place is not always an obstacle. Some buyers purchase occupied rentals, and some owners would rather sell the house empty. If the lease is month-to-month or the tenant has stopped paying, how and when to end the tenancy will affect the timeline, so talk to a licensed Alabama attorney about the notice that fits your facts.

Is a cash sale of a tenant-occupied house possible?

It can be. A cash buyer does not wait on mortgage underwriting or an appraisal, and an investor who buys rentals can take on a house in the condition it is in.

That includes houses with deferred repairs under the landlord's duties, late-paying tenants and mixed paperwork. The seller still has to be honest about the lease, the tenant's status and any notice that has been served. If you would rather close and move on, you can ask for an offer on the house as it stands and decide afterward. There is nothing owed if you say no.

More questions about Alabama Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

How much notice does an Alabama landlord give for unpaid rent?

The landlord delivers a written notice stating the rent and late fees owed, with termination not less than seven business days after the tenant receives it. If the tenant pays the amount in that window, the lease does not end.

Can a tenant fix a lease violation after getting a notice?

Usually yes, within the notice period. The statute caps cures at two per 12 months without the landlord's written consent, and some acts such as drug use, certain firearm violations and criminal assault cannot be cured.

What repairs must an Alabama landlord make?

The landlord must follow health and safety codes, keep the unit habitable, maintain electrical, plumbing, heating and cooling systems and supplied appliances, handle garbage removal, and supply running water, reasonable hot water and reasonable heat, with limited exceptions.

Does a buyer of a rental take over the landlord's disclosure duty?

The statute says the disclosure duty extends to and is enforceable against any successor landlord, owner or manager, and the information must stay current.

Can a tenant agree to maintain the house?

For a single-family home, yes, by a written agreement covering garbage, water and specified repairs. For other dwellings, the agreement needs a separate signed writing and cannot cover work needed to cure a code violation.

Where is squatting covered?

In Chapter 9B of Title 35, which is separate from the landlord and tenant act in Chapter 9A.

Alabama Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

  • Alabama Eviction Notice Rules: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Alabama Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Alabama Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Alabama House? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Material lease violation (or health/safety noncompliance under 35-9A-301): written notice with termination date not less than seven business days after receipt; tenant may cure before that date; an intentional material misrepresentation in the lease or application may not be cured. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-421(a); source)
  • No lease breach may be cured more than two times in a 12-month period without landlord's written consent; certain noncurable defaults (illegal drugs, illegal firearm use, criminal assault, repeat same breach within six months) allow termination on seven-day notice. (Ala. Code § 35-9A-421(d); source)
Selling in Alabama?
We buy Alabama houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How many days of notice must an Alabama landlord give before evicting?

It depends on the reason, and the shortest period in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is seven days. The longest common one is 30 days, for ending a month-to-month tenancy without any stated cause.

The table below pulls the periods from the sections of the Alabama Code that govern them.

SituationNoticeSection
Unpaid rentWritten notice naming rent and late fees owed; lease ends not less than seven business days after receipt if unpaid35-9A-421(b)
Material lease breach or health and safety violationWritten notice naming the acts; termination date not less than seven business days after receipt35-9A-421(a)
Noncurable default (listed acts)Seven day notice, no right to cure unless the landlord agrees35-9A-421(d)
Week-to-week tenancyWritten notice at least seven days before the termination date35-9A-441(a)
Month-to-month tenancyWritten notice at least 30 days before the periodic rental date35-9A-441(b)

A notice is a written step that comes before any court filing. The lawsuit itself is covered separately on our Alabama eviction process page.

What must a nonpayment notice say in Alabama?

It must be written, delivered to the tenant, and state the amount of rent and any late fees owed. Section 35-9A-421(b) says the notice must also state that the rental agreement will end on a date not less than seven business days after the tenant receives it.

If the tenant pays what the notice demands within that period, the breach is cured and the lease continues. If not, the rental agreement terminates under the statute, and the landlord can go to court for possession.

When a tenant's conduct breaks the lease in two ways at once, for example unpaid rent and a material breach, the statute says the seven day nonpayment period governs. A landlord therefore does not need to run two separate clocks.

What is a notice for a material lease violation?

It is a written notice that lists the acts or omissions that make up the breach and sets a termination date at least seven business days after receipt. Section 35-9A-421(a) applies to material noncompliance with the rental agreement, to an intentional misrepresentation of a material fact in the lease or application, and to a failure to meet the tenant's health and safety duties under Section 35-9A-301.

The tenant may fix the breach before the termination date and, if the fix is adequate, the lease does not end. One kind of violation cannot be fixed at all: an intentional misrepresentation of a material fact in the rental agreement or application.

The landlord can also seek actual damages and reasonable attorney fees, and an injunction, for the tenant's noncompliance under Section 35-9A-421(c).

Which lease violations allow a seven day notice with no chance to cure?

Four kinds of conduct count as noncurable defaults under Section 35-9A-421(d), and for these the landlord may terminate on a seven-day notice. The list says it includes, but is not limited to, the acts below.

  • Manufacturing, growing, importing, transporting, possessing, supplying, administering or using illegal drugs in the unit or common areas.
  • Illegal use, manufacture, import, possession, supply or discharge of a firearm or ammunition on the rental property, except in self-defense, defense of another or as allowed by Section 13A-3-23.
  • Criminal assault of a tenant or guest on the property, with the same self-defense exceptions.
  • A second breach with substantially the same acts as one the tenant already cured, if it happens within six months.

The same subsection limits cures generally. A tenant may not cure the breach of any lease term more than two times in a 12 month period unless the landlord consents in writing, and this applies notwithstanding Section 35-9A-141.

How does a landlord end a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy?

By written notice, with 30 days for a month-to-month tenancy and seven days for a week-to-week tenancy. Section 35-9A-441 lets either the landlord or the tenant give the notice, so a tenant who wants to leave uses the same periods.

The 30 days are measured back from the periodic rental date written in the notice. A landlord who wants a tenant out by the first of a month should give the notice at least 30 days before that date.

This route needs no allegation of wrongdoing. It suits an owner who is selling and simply needs the house empty, and it can be combined with a buyer's closing date when the dates line up.

What happens if a tenant stays after the notice period ends?

The landlord may bring an action for possession, and if the tenant's holdover is willful and not in good faith, the landlord may recover more. Section 35-9A-441(c) allows an amount equal to not more than three months' periodic rent, or the landlord's actual damages if those are greater, plus reasonable attorney fees.

There is a counterweight. If the landlord consents to the tenant's continued occupancy, a different rule, Section 35-9A-161(d), governs.

Court steps after that point, including service, the seven day appeal window and the writ, are the subject of a separate page.

Can a landlord send a notice in response to a complaint?

Not if the notice is retaliation. Section 35-9A-501 bars a landlord from increasing rent in a discriminatory way, cutting services, or bringing or threatening an action for possession because the tenant took one of three protected steps.

  • The tenant complained to a government agency charged with enforcing a building or housing code about a violation materially affecting health and safety.
  • The tenant complained to the landlord about a violation of the landlord's duty to maintain the premises under Section 35-9A-204.
  • The tenant organized or joined a tenants' union or similar group.

A tenant who proves retaliation has the remedies in Section 35-9A-407 and a defense against the possession case. The landlord can still sue when the tenant is in default on rent, when the tenant or a guest caused the code violation by lack of reasonable care, when repairs would effectively deprive the tenant of the home, or for other material lease violations.

What does the landlord owe the tenant after the tenancy ends?

Any security deposit that is not used must come back with an itemized list of what was withheld, within 60 days. Section 35-9A-201 says the landlord may apply the deposit to unpaid rent and to damages caused by the tenant's failure to meet Section 35-9A-301, and must deliver an itemized written notice with the balance 60 days after the tenancy ends and possession is delivered.

A landlord may not demand more than one month's periodic rent as security, except for pets, changes to the premises or increased liability risks.

An owner planning a sale should put that 60 day deadline on the calendar.

Does a notice make it easier to sell the house?

A properly served notice gives an owner a date to plan around, and some buyers will wait for it. Others will not buy until the tenant has left.

We buy Alabama houses in many conditions, including rentals where a notice is out or a case is pending. Send us the address and where you are in the process, and we can talk about a closing date that fits your timeline.

More questions about Alabama Eviction Notice Rules

How long is an Alabama eviction notice for unpaid rent?

Section 35-9A-421(b) requires a written notice stating the rent and late fees owed, with termination not less than seven business days after the tenant receives it.

How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in Alabama?

At least 30 days, in writing, before the periodic rental date named in the notice, under Section 35-9A-441(b). Either landlord or tenant can give it.

Can an Alabama landlord skip the cure period?

For certain acts, yes. Section 35-9A-421(d) lists drug activity, illegal firearm use, criminal assault and a repeat of a cured breach within six months as noncurable and allows seven-day termination.

How many times can a tenant cure the same lease problem?

No breach may be cured more than two times in any 12 month period without the landlord's written consent, according to Section 35-9A-421(d).

What can a landlord recover from a tenant who stays after the notice?

If the holdover is willful and not in good faith, up to three months' periodic rent or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney fees under Section 35-9A-441(c).

When does a landlord have to return the deposit in Alabama?

Within 60 days after the tenancy ends and possession is delivered, with an itemized list of any amounts withheld, under Section 35-9A-201.
